newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian army could collapse into chaos, group says.
newsitem.headline: Russian army could collapse into chaos, group says.

text.p: Russia's underfinanced army is in such poor shape it could collapse, prompting a military coup or civil war, a non-government research group said on Friday.

"The army has long ceased to be a guarantee against external threats," the Council for Foreign and Defence Policy think-tank said in a statement published in the liberal Nezavisimaya Gazeta newspaper.
"The present state of the Russian army can be described only as a catastrophe of the armed forces which...is growing into a national catastrophe."
The council groups political analysts, parliamentary deputies, business leaders and journalists.

"Within the next three years the army, if it is not reformed, will disappear as such, or it will break up into armed groups which make ends meet through selling arms or robberies, or there could be a military coup which could grow into dictatorship or civil war," the statement said.
Russia's top brass has also issued warnings about the sorry state of the army, once regarded in Moscow with immense pride and respect.

"If things go on like this for another two years we may have a navy without ships, an airforce without planes and a military industry incapable of producing modern weapons," Yuri Baturin, secretary of President Boris Yeltsin's advisory Defence Council said last week.
Defence Minister Igor Rodionov cautioned last week that Moscow's vast nuclear arsenal, which helped establish the Soviet Union as a superpower during the Cold War, could become "uncontrollable".
He said the state of the armed forces was "horrifying".
To some extent, the remarks reflect public lobbying by the once very private military to win support and funding.
After his nuclear warning last week, Rodionov was granted an audience with Yeltsin, who has a strictly limited schedule of meetings to ease his recovery from pneumonia.
The two are due to meet on Monday.
Russia has been seeking for several years to launch military reforms but they have partly been blocked by differences over what shape the changes should take.
Many Russian soldiers and officers are underpaid, underfed and poorly clothed, suffering from wage delays affecting millions of workers across Russia.
There has been a series of scandals over corruption and misappropriation of weapons.
The Council for Foreign and Defence Policy said costly military reforms, such as Yeltsin's promise to replace Russia's conscript army with a professional force, could not start yet.
It suggested civilians should have overall charge of the armed forces and the military should devise a way to keep experienced commanders from leaving for better-paid jobs.
Its leaders should outline genuine needs to keep the force intact, rather than draw up an expensive wish list, the think-tank said.
